title: What Changed When We Fixed the Data
dek: We refreshed the MyAnimeList catalog behind ANIME after Jikan shut down, moved to the Tenrai-compatible API, and recomputed every headline on the clean TV frame. The light-novel reach premium fell from 32× to 27.5×; manga's 8.0+ share fell to 14.8%; 2015 isekai was under-counted at 0.9% (now 2.2%).
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: LN vs original median members on TV (was 32.0×)
manga TV titles scoring 8.0+ (was 17.0%)
isekai-tagged TV share in 2015 (was 0.9%); 2021 still 20.4%

ps: Executive summary. The ANIME report's core story survives on the October 2026 ledger: source material still sets the audience floor, and isekai tags trace a real production wave. What changed is measurement. When MyAnimeList's public Jikan mirror shut down on 2026-10-01, we finished the refresh through Tenrai (api.tenrai.org, Jikan-compatible) and recomputed every headline on anime_2026-10-11_clean with one script. The light-novel reach multiple narrows from 32.0× to 27.5×. Manga's high-score share falls from 17.0% to 14.8%. The 2015 isekai point was an under-tag in the old exploratory frame (0.9% → 2.2%); 2021 stays 20.4% and 2024 edges to 18.1%. Single-year shares are trends, not precise point estimates — bootstrap ranges are about ±5 percentage points.

The published report rested on the TidyTuesday export of 2019-04-23 (13,631 unique titles). A parallel pipeline had already grown the catalog to 18,818 rows with AniList tags, streaming links, and season fields. On 2026-10-01, MyAnimeList discontinued the free Jikan v4 API (api.jikan.moe). We completed metadata fetches through Tenrai, which mirrors the same Jikan field schema, then ran scripts/anime-data/clean_audit.py (seed 20261011) to produce anime_2026-10-11_clean.* with documented inclusion rules and bootstrap ranges.
Published / exploratory is what readers saw before this audit. Clean new is the October 2026 TV frame from the clean file; brackets are 95% bootstrap ranges where shown.

fig.cap: Grey: published or exploratory figures. Blue: October 2026 clean TV frame.

ps: We drew n = 200 rows with both Tenrai/Jikan and AniList fields present (seed 20261011). Score agreement within 0.5 points on the MAL 0–10 scale (|MAL − AniList meanScore/10| ≤ 0.5): 146 / 200 = 73%. This is an offline check of already-joined fields — not a live re-fetch at audit time. Year agreement between aired_from_year and season_year was weaker (59.5%), which is why calendar-year shares carry wide bootstrap bands.

Cleaning removed 5 rows missing id/name, normalized source labels, and nulled five end-before-start dates. No scores were imputed. Full PRISMA counts and rules R1–R7 are in data/anime/CLEANING_LOG.md.

For any one premiere year, the 95% bootstrap interval is typically about ±5 percentage points around the point estimate. That is wide enough that 17.7% vs 18.1% for 2024 isekai should be read as still elevated after the 2021 peak, not as proof of a 0.4-point decline. The charts in the main report show the full 2010–2025 trend lines and stacked source mix instead of over-interpreting one year.

ps: Executive summary. Research is only as good as its ledger, so we treat corrections as findings. We re-audited the data behind PADRES: Record Sale, Zero Championships, fixed a broken sync to the live HTML body, and recomputed every number we had published. The thesis survives: demand and tax payroll are solved; conversion is not; franchise values still track the market. What changed is the calendar. The sale is approved. Milwaukee ended 2026. The FAQ no longer claims eight runs in two winner-take-all games.

The July 2026 live page in src/content/blog/padres.md had lost four sections (Fifty-seven seasons, Preller doctrine, tax-bill section, expansion peers), spliced the expansion “alibi” paragraph onto the Wrigley opener, and left charts 1, 3, and 4 without working embeds. audioSrc pointed at /audios/padres.mp3 (SPA fallback) instead of /audios/padres-the-artometrics-of-paying-for-october.mp3. The Quarto source at articles/padres/ was intact; the publish merge was not.

We rebuilt the numeric ledger from Lahman’s 2025 database (Padres 1969–2025, CC BY-SA 3.0), added the completed 2026 season from Baseball-Reference, and fact-checked 91–71 against the MLB Stats API NL standings (see data/padres/verify/mlb_api_check.json). Competitive-balance-tax payrolls remain the Spotrac compilation in the July 2026 draft—labeled as tax payroll, not cash. One script reproduces the clean tables: python3 scripts/padres-data/clean_audit.py (rules in CLEANING_LOG.md, intervals in METHODS_NOTE.md).

Published is what the July 2026 live page or sports-canon generator stated. Raw new recomputes from Lahman without changing the file. Clean new is the October 2026 audit, including 2026 and copy fixes. Brackets on rates are 95% bootstrap ranges (5,000 draws, seed 20261013).
The full machine-readable ledger is data/padres/clean/old_vs_new.csv (mirrored under public/data/articles/padres/data/).

Calendar, not math. Lahman through 2025 was already correct on wins, attendance, and the 132/116/11 coin-flip split. The step change is 2026: a third straight postseason, a wild-card sweep of the Cubs, and an NLDS loss to the Brewers—the club the July draft had used as a low-payroll alibi.

Copy and sync, not sources. The eight-run FAQ line had no box-score support (Games 4–5 of the 2024 NLDS were shutouts; the 2025 wild-card deciding game was 1–3). The sale paragraph was stale after the unanimous August vote. The pennant-gap chart mislabeled the first bar; the axis now distinguishes debut-to-first-pennant from gaps between flags.
Wording on payroll. Summing six Spotrac competitive-balance-tax payrolls is not the same as cash spent. The report now says $1,500.1 million of tax payroll, with 2026 still a July snapshot.

title: What Changed When We Fixed the Data
dek: We audited the franchise dataset behind our FRANCHISE report, rebuilt it from Wikipedia's October 2026 list and recomputed every published number. Merchandise still dominates (55.8%), but the Japan–US ranking flipped and Hello Kitty's $80B was a source error.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: sampled 2019 franchises within 10% of their own Wikipedia source
merchandise share, essentially unchanged from 56.0%
box office share, mostly a measurement change

ps: Executive summary. Research is only as good as its ledger, so we treat corrections as findings. We re-audited the data behind FRANCHISE: Merchandise Owns the Ledger, rebuilt it from Wikipedia's October 2026 list, and recomputed every number we had published. The core finding survives: merchandise is still 55.8% of franchise revenue. Three readings change. Box office looks twice as big, but mostly because it is now counted more completely. Ownership is more concentrated (top five parents 58.2%, up from 46.4%). And the Japan–US comparison reverses.

The original report used the TidyTuesday file of July 2, 2019: 321 rows, 103 franchises, eight revenue categories. It had no missing values or duplicates, but it had 15 placeholder rows under $10 million (Star Wars TV at $0.004B), six cells with leftover Wikipedia citation tags, 59 with stray double spaces, and owner names from 2019 (AT&T, Viacom, Activision Blizzard).

We then checked it against the source it was scraped from — the Wikipedia revision of June 29, 2019 — for a random sample of 40 franchises (seed 20261012). Thirty-nine matched. Only 5 agreed with the itemised breakdown within 1%, and 28 of 39 came within 10% of the headline total. The file was always lower, because its eight-category schema dropped line items that did not fit: card games, theme parks, pachinko. James Bond is the extreme case at $13.9B against $19.9B.

fig.cap: Every sampled franchise sits on or below the line: the 2019 file under-counts its own source.

ps: Published is the number in the report before October 2026. Raw new recomputes it from the unchanged 2019 file (every figure reproduces exactly). Clean new uses the rebuilt October 2026 ledger; brackets are 95% bootstrap ranges. Dollar figures are USD billions, nominal.

fig.cap: Grey: published 2019 figure. Blue: October 2026. Pokémon, Call of Duty, Naruto and the MCU grew; Hello Kitty, Mario and Gundam were revised at the source.

ps: Source revisions, not declines. Hello Kitty ($80.0B→$33.5B), Mario ($35.0B→$9.74B) and Gundam ($25.5B→$5.0B) fell because Wikipedia editors replaced older estimates with better-sourced ones. Neither Sanrio nor Nintendo reported a collapse. We flag these rows rather than quote them as change.
Real growth. Pokémon (+$39.8B), Call of Duty (+$14.0B) and Naruto (+$13.9B) added seven years of sales and newly itemised mobile revenue.

Measurement. Box office went from 8.9% to 18.3% of the ledger. On the 82 franchises in both vintages it is 15.4%, and on franchises above $4B it is 15.0%. Most of the jump is the 2026 list counting theatrical grosses more completely.

Coverage. The list grew from 103 to 140. Forty-three of the 58 additions are US-origin (Fortnite, Avatar, Madden NFL), while Japanese titles such as Detective Conan, Digimon and Bleach left the English table. Together with the downward revisions, that turns “Japan out-earns the US” into “the US out-earns Japan, and Japan is more merchandise-heavy.”

Consolidation. Assigning franchises to today's parents (Activision Blizzard and King into Microsoft, Fox into Disney, Viacom into Paramount Skydance) lifts the top-five share. On the same 2019 franchises it would be 62.8%.

title: Merchandise Owns the Ledger
dek: 140 franchises on the October 2026 Wikipedia ledger sum to $1.45T lifetime revenue. Merchandise is 55.8%; box office 18.3%; Pokémon leads at $130.7B. The US now out-earns Japan ($816B vs $394B), but Japan runs the higher merchandise share (71.4% vs 52.0%). Nine of 2025's ten biggest films were franchise entries.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: lifetime revenue, 140 franchises (Wikipedia, Oct 12 2026, S017)
merchandise, licensing & retail share (95% range 44.0–66.2)
Pokémon, more than Star Wars and the MCU combined ($84.2B)

ps: Executive summary. Franchise economics is licensing geometry: who owns repeatable rights, and which revenue streams compound after the premiere. On Wikipedia's October 2026 ledger (140 properties, $1,448.1B lifetime, S017), merchandise, licensing and retail are 55.8% of revenue; box office is 18.3% and games 17.9%. Pokémon leads at $130.7B — more than Star Wars ($46.7B) and the Marvel Cinematic Universe ($37.5B) combined. Consolidated to today's parents, Disney holds 29.7% of the ledger and five companies hold 58.2%. The regional story flipped when we rebuilt the data: US-origin franchises now out-earn Japan's ($816.5B vs $394.5B), but Japan's are the purer merchandise machines (71.4% vs 52.0%). In theaters the sequel economy deepened — franchise installments took 94.4% of 2025's worldwide top-ten gross. Several big 2019 figures (Hello Kitty $80.0B, Mario $35.0B) were source errors, not declines; the companion piece “What changed when we fixed the data” documents every revision.

A child trades a cardboard Pikachu for lunch money; Bob Iger signs a seventy-one-point-three-billion-dollar check for Twenty-First Century Fox. Both trades assume the same premise — that characters can be mined long after opening weekend. Our x-ray is Wikipedia's “highest-grossing media franchises” list as of October 12, 2026 (revision 1379832186, S017): 140 franchises, each itemised into revenue streams that we map to one standard schema. The earlier edition of this report used the TidyTuesday file of July 2, 2019 (103 franchises, S001); we keep it as a baseline and audited it against the Wikipedia revision it was scraped from. Figures are editors' lifetime estimates of consumer spend in nominal dollars, not audited studio financials — still the cleanest public ledger for comparing how money attaches to IP.

custom:
Franchise · Data brief

Merchandise owns the ledger

What 140 franchises on Wikipedia’s October 2026 list say about IP, Disney and the sequel economy.

By Kyle McAuliffe · Oct 12, 2026 · 5 min

One ledger

A child trades a cardboard Pikachu for lunch money. Bob Iger signs a $71.3 billion check for 21st Century Fox. Both trades rest on the same premise: characters can be mined long after opening weekend.

Our x-ray is Wikipedia’s list of the highest-grossing media franchises as of October 12, 2026: 140 franchises, each split into revenue streams. Together they total $1,448.1 billion in lifetime revenue. These are editors’ estimates of consumer spending in nominal dollars, not audited studio financials. Still, it is the cleanest public ledger for comparing how money attaches to IP.

The cinema is the ad

Merchandise, licensing and retail bring in $809.4 billion, or 55.8% of the ledger. Box office is 18.3% and video games 17.9%. At franchise scale, the theatrical release is usually marketing. The toys, cards and park tickets carry the money.

Box office looks twice as big as in the 2019 file (18.3% versus 8.9%), but that is mostly measurement: today’s list itemises film grosses more fully. Restricted to the 82 franchises in both years, it is 15.4%.

Pokémon, then everyone

Pokémon leads at $130.7 billion, of which $119.3 billion is retail sales. That is more than Star Wars and the Marvel Cinematic Universe combined ($84.2 billion). The anime promotes the cards; the cards promote the games. In the 2019 file Pokémon was $90.9 billion.

Five parents, 58%

58.2%

Assign each franchise to its 2026 parent company and Disney alone holds $430.7 billion, or 29.7% of the ledger. The top five (Disney, Warner Bros. Discovery, The Pokémon Company, Microsoft and Paramount Skydance) hold 58.2%. The previous edition put the top five at 46.4%; most of the rise is consolidation, such as Microsoft’s $69 billion Activision purchase in 2023.

Audited numbers tell the same story. Disney’s fiscal 2024 Form 10-K reports Experiences, its parks, cruises and consumer products, at $34.2 billion, against $41.2 billion for Entertainment. The characters promoted on screen get paid again at the turnstile. That is what the big checks bought: Pixar for $7.4 billion, Marvel for $4.0 billion, Lucasfilm for $4.05 billion.

The flip

The 2019 file said Japan out-earned the US. On the rebuilt ledger, US-origin franchises total $816.5 billion against Japan’s $394.5 billion. But Japan’s are the purer merchandise machines: 71.4% of their revenue comes from goods, against 52.0% for the US.

Two things moved. The list grew from 103 to 140 franchises, with many US additions such as Fortnite and Avatar. And several Japanese totals were revised down at the source: Hello Kitty fell from $80.0 billion to $33.5 billion, and Mario from $35.0 billion to $9.74 billion. Sanrio and Nintendo reported no collapse. Treat “the US out-earns Japan” as a fact about this English-language list, not about national industries.

Japan’s production committees explain part of the gap. They split copyright among publishers, broadcasters and toy makers, which builds plush, magazines and cards into the budget from day one.

A sequel chart

9 of 10

Nine of 2025’s ten biggest films worldwide were franchise installments, taking 94.4% of top-ten gross, led by Ne Zha 2 ($2.32 billion) and Zootopia 2 ($1.87 billion). F1 was the only original. 2026 is different so far: franchises hold 62.0%, with The Odyssey ($1.78 billion) and Michael ($1.03 billion) among the originals. Several 2026 titles are still in theaters.

For a buyer

Franchise economics rewards objects you can sell again and again more than minutes in a theater. So name the vintage, name the parent, and check whether a big move is a market change or just a source revision.

■ END

Sources

  1. Wikipedia, List of highest-grossing media franchises, rev. 1379832186, Oct 12 2026 (S017).
  2. TidyTuesday, Media Franchise Revenues, 2019-07-02 (S001).
  3. Wikipedia, 2025 in film (rev. 1378645325) and 2026 in film (rev. 1379926625), citing Box Office Mojo and The Numbers.
  4. Hernández Hernández, Á. D. (2018). Production committees. Arts 7(3): 42.
  5. The Walt Disney Company, Form 10-K FY2024, segment revenues (S004, S081).
  6. Full report, methods and data: artometrics.com/franchise · repo folder.

title: Record Sale, Zero Championships
dek: San Diego solved demand and the tax bill. It has not solved October. Franchise values follow the market and the ballpark anyway.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: owners approved the sale unanimously; José E. Feliciano is the control person
2026 record, second in the NL West; wild-card sweep of the Cubs, NLDS loss to the Brewers

ps: San Diego solved the two problems a mid-market club is supposed to fail. The park is full. The tax bill is paid. October is still close to a coin flip, and the franchise is on the wrong side of it. The market is paying a record price anyway. Franchise values follow the city and the building, not the trophy case.
Five findings, for an owner, a lender, or the league office.

The May agreement and the August vote are the same transaction seen from two desks. The family agreed to transfer control. The owners then approved it, unanimously, on a conference call on August 17, 2026. Major League Baseball's release said closing remained contingent on the weeks ahead; NBC 7 San Diego reported the new group could take operational control by the end of that week, with a press conference at Petco Park on August 24.

The red bars are the postseasons: 1984, 1996, 1998, 2005, 2006, 2020, 2022, 2024, 2025, and now 2026. The diamonds are the pennants. There are two of them. The hatched bar is 2026, which Lahman does not yet contain. Baseball-Reference has the club at 91–71, second in the National League West; a wild-card win over the Cubs, 2–0; and a division-series loss to Milwaukee, 3–1. The Brewers finished 103–59 in the regular season on the same site.

fig.cap: Ten Octobers in 58 seasons

ps: Wins and attendance do not move together. The cloud sits all over the chart. The step that matters is 2004, the first Petco Park season in the file: 3,016,752, after 2,030,084 the year before. The 2023, 2024, and 2025 seasons then set franchise records, ending at 3,437,201. Lemke, Leonard, and Tlhokwane (2010) treat attendance as a mix of team quality, weather, and promotions. San Diego's chart says the building did more work than the standings. Siegfried and Zimbalist (2000) and the later survey by Bradbury, Coates, and Humphreys (2023) are the caution on the public side of that building: stadiums rarely pay a city back. Erie, Kogan, and MacKenzie (2011) is the San Diego account of how Petco was financed. The dollar split of that deal is not reprinted here.

fig.cap: The park filled without a title

sections.h: The Preller doctrine and the tax bill
ps: A.J. Preller has run baseball operations since 2014, and the August approval left him there. The method, as the club has practiced it, is to buy the present with the future. The pattern is the contracts on Machado, Tatis, and Bogaerts, and the 2022 trade that sent a Washington package including James Wood, MacKenzie Gore, and CJ Abrams for Juan Soto, who was then moved on. Dollar figures for those deals are not restated here. The win totals are in Lahman: 70 in 2019, 37 in the 60-game 2020 season, 79, 89, 82, 93, and 90 from 2021 through 2025. The floor rose. The pennant did not.

fig.cap: The tax bill bought October access

sections.h: October is a lottery. San Diego still trails it
ps: One hundred thirty-two, one hundred sixteen, eleven. That is the league's October from 1995 through 2025, once each series is tagged with the two clubs' regular-season winning percentages. The better club wins a little more than half the time when the percentages differ, and not more than that. Lopez, Matthews, and Baumer supply the reason to expect this. Baseball's season is long and its playoff is short. Randomness has room.
The useful clubs are not the Dodgers. Los Angeles is the outspend case, and this file does not contain a 2026 Dodgers payroll. The useful clubs are the ones that did something San Diego has not.

What to watch, in order. The closing. The final 2026 tax payroll, once someone has the export. The farm list, once FanGraphs or Baseball America is on the desk, because the July "last of 30" is not repeated blind. The guarantees on the long contracts, for the same reason. And the labor negotiation, because the threshold line on the payroll chart is a rule, and the rule expires.

title: When Dynasties Are Systems
dek: Yankees, Patriots, Celtics, Cowboys: a synthesis of Artometrics' sports-dynasty reports asks what transfers when winning is a system, not a roster.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: Yankees World Series titles at a 40% Finals conversion rate
Patriots Super Bowl championships in 19 seasons, a 55% conversion rate across 9 appearances
Celtics NBA championships, the league record entering 2025, with 11 in the Russell era

ps: Three Artometrics reports already established the raw numbers: the Yankees' 27 World Series titles, the Patriots' six Super Bowls in 19 seasons, and the Celtics' 18 NBA championships, the league record entering 2025. None of those reports asked the question this one does — what, if anything, transfers across sports when a dynasty outlives the star who built it, and where does spending alone fail to substitute for it.

This is the framework's actual contribution — an editorial typology, not a new measurement. Two of the three source reports describe dynasties whose championship archives outlived their most famous single star. The sports-dynasty index's own sibling pieces on the Lakers ("how the Lakers convert star gravity into title eras") and the Warriors ("the franchise that rewrote basketball offense") describe a different mechanism: championship output that tracks the presence of a specific, dominant talent core. Call that star-gravity. The Patriots and Celtics reports describe something else: system dynasties, where coaching, front-office structure, or multi-generational institutional identity keeps producing championships across rosters that do not share a single defining star. The Patriots won six titles under one quarterback-coach pairing; the Celtics won 18 across five distinct eras — Russell, Havlicek, Bird, Pierce/Garnett, and Tatum/Brown, per the Celtics report's own era buckets — a continuity no single star's career could span.

fig.cap: Championship mass is not evenly distributed across the four cited franchises

sections.h: When spending doesn't convert: Cowboys and Padres
ps: The sports-dynasty index's third finding is the cleanest evidence against treating market value as a proxy for competitive output: the Cowboys have won zero Super Bowls since their 1990s dynasty ended in 1996, despite ranking in the top five of NFL franchise valuations every year since. The same report cites the Maple Leafs' 57-season active Stanley Cup drought entering 2025 as the longest among high-value franchises in any of the four leagues it compares. Elsewhere in the Artometrics archive, the Padres report frames the same failure in dollar terms — a reported $3.9bn in spending against zero championships. None of these three cases lack resources. What they lack, by the sports-dynasty index's own framing, is whatever the Patriots and Celtics reports describe as the system: a repeatable institutional mechanism for converting access — Finals appearances, playoff berths, big-name signings — into titles. Spending buys attention and access. It does not, on this evidence, buy conversion.

fig.cap: Spending does not shorten a drought: three franchises, three unrelated timers

sections.h: The Patriots test: what survives the star's departure
ps: The Patriots report's own numbers are the strongest system-dynasty case in the corpus: six championships and nine Super Bowl appearances between 2001 and 2019, a 55% conversion rate — 6 of 11 all-time Super Bowl appearances — that the sports-dynasty index singles out as the highest among dynasty-tier franchises since 1950. That conversion rate exceeds even the Yankees' 40%, despite the Yankees holding more than four times the total championship count. The Patriots report itself frames 2020 — the first season without Tom Brady — as the hinge point where brand capital stayed high while football output did not automatically follow. That report leaves the question open rather than answering it: whether the infrastructure (coaching continuity, personnel evaluation, a specific institutional culture) survives the departure of the star who anchored it. This synthesis does not resolve that question with new data; it names it as the central test case for the star-gravity vs. system distinction, because the Patriots dynasty is the one cited case in the corpus where the star left and the institution kept operating without him.

fig.cap: Patriots converted Super Bowl trips at a higher rate than the Yankees converted World Series trips

ps: Across the three source reports, championship mass, conversion efficiency, and institutional durability turn out to be separate variables, not one. The Yankees carry the largest archive without the highest conversion rate; the Patriots carry the highest conversion rate on a much smaller archive; the Celtics carry both a large archive and a proven ability to survive a 22-year interruption. The Cowboys and, per the Padres report, the Padres show that none of this is guaranteed by spending alone.

title: The Cost of Being the Product
dek: A Psychonomics profile of Michael Jackson — Thriller's 34× RIAA certification, the 2016 Sony/ATV deal, and the disputed allegations on the same ledger.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: Thriller's RIAA certification, the most-certified album in RIAA history
Sony's reported 2016 buyout of the Jackson estate's 50% stake in Sony/ATV Music Publishing
Forbes-reported 2016 earnings for the Jackson estate, at the time the highest single-year figure Forbes had recorded for any celebrity

ps: Economics manages the house. Psychonomics asks who manages the soul of the house — and what that architecture costs. Julius Caesar scaled the self into a state, absorbed by patronage. Beyoncé scaled the self into a firm, governed by Parkwood. Michael Jackson scaled the self into a product: the catalog was the body, Neverland was the household myth, and the public was invited to consume both directly, for decades, without a clean line between the artist and the object for sale.

Jackson's coded profile is not Caesar's shape (near-ceiling power, near-floor distrust) or Beyoncé's shape (ceiling task and control with an owned firm at the center). It spikes hardest on Need for Affiliation (A = 0.93) — the documented, career-long drive to be loved by an audience directly, at scale — paired with Task Orientation (T = 0.88), visible in the meticulous, self-directed control Jackson exercised over choreography, production, and stagecraft. Belief in Ability to Control Events (B = 0.84) is also elevated, consistent with a performer who treated the show, the image, and eventually the estate as things that could be engineered. Need for Power (P = 0.62) and Conceptual Complexity (CC = 0.58) sit closer to the baseline; this is not a profile built around institutional or political power. Read this way, Jackson's psychonomic argument is not "the self as institution" (Caesar) or "the self as firm" (Beyoncé). It is the self as the thing being sold directly to an audience it needed to love it back — a performer-affiliation shape rather than a governance shape. That is the interpretive hinge for the rest of this report: when affiliation this high is the organizing need, the persona and the product become very hard to separate, for the audience and for the person.

fig.cap: This is an editorial/interpretive index, not measured data: Jackson's coded profile spikes on Need for Affiliation (A = 0.93) and Task Orientation (T = 0.88), well above the world-leader reference baseline, while Need for Power (P = 0.62) sits closer to baseline.

ps: Thriller was released in 1982 and is RIAA-certified 34× Platinum as of the RIAA's most recent certification update — the best-certified album in the organization's history. That certification measures units, not years, but the years matter here: it kept accumulating long after 1982, through re-releases, catalog streaming, and the posthumous attention that followed Jackson's 2009 death. In March 2016, Sony bought out the Jackson estate's 50% stake in the Sony/ATV Music Publishing catalog for a reported $750 million, as widely reported at the time by Reuters and Billboard. That same year, Forbes' "Top-Earning Dead Celebrities" list reported the Jackson estate earning $825 million in 2016 — at the time, the highest single-year figure Forbes had ever recorded for any celebrity, living or dead. Those three numbers sit on different units — a certification count and two dollar figures seven years apart in origin but landing in the same calendar year — and this report does not collapse them into one index. What they show together is a catalog that behaved, financially, as if the person behind it were still actively productive: a 2016 valuation event and a 2016 earnings record, both keyed to a body of work made mostly in the 1980s. The commercial afterlife did not simply persist; at points it out-earned the living-era peak years.

fig.cap: Thriller's 34× Platinum RIAA certification is the highest of any album in RIAA history; the same catalog underwrote a $750 million 2016 Sony/ATV sale and an $825 million single-year estate-earnings record.

ps: If Beyoncé is control of the house, Jackson is what happens when the house is the product. The two charts above do not share an axis, and that is not an oversight — it is the finding. The commercial ledger (Chart 1) shows a catalog that kept generating peak-scale value in 2016, seven years after Jackson's death and roughly two decades after the criminal case that dominated public attention in 2003–2005. The legal ledger (Chart 2) shows a set of dated events — an undisclosed 1994 settlement, a 2005 acquittal, a 2009 death, a 2019 documentary — that never produced a criminal conviction, but also never fully receded from public discussion.

title: The Field Guide Culture Workers Needed
dek: A working framework for treating economic narratives as contagious, falsifiable objects — built from Shiller and Kuran, not a proprietary dataset.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: Publication year of Robert Shiller's "Narrative Economics," the book that treats popular stories as contagious economic objects
Publication year of Timur Kuran's "Private Truths, Public Lies," the source of the preference-falsification concept used here
Worked cases applying the framework: crypto, the pandemic, meme stocks, and celebrity scandal

ps: Everyone in culture and business says "the narrative changed." Almost nobody can define a narrative as an economic object with a shape, a lifespan, and a falsifier. Robert Shiller's narrative economics treats popular stories as contagious — with something like an infection phase, mutation into new slogans, and eventual burnout — that move markets and institutions independent of whether the underlying facts are true. This is the briefing note for culture workers tired of vibes language.
Four terms carry the whole piece, and they are used precisely, not loosely:

sections.h: Crypto Fights Its Own Counter-Narrative, Not Just the Market
ps: Crypto's central narrative pairing is "digital gold" against "tulip mania." Neither slogan is a data point; each is a compressed argument standing in for a longer case — one for scarcity-as-store-of-value, one for speculative mania with no fundamental floor. Shiller's framework predicts exactly this shape: a dominant narrative provokes a counter-narrative that borrows the same contagious mechanics, and the two compete for the same finite pool of attention rather than debating on a shared evidentiary ledger. Whichever slogan is easier to retell at a given moment — not whichever is more accurate — tends to win the news cycle. The operator lesson is to measure slogan volume, not theology. An analyst who tries to adjudicate whether crypto "really is" digital gold is answering the wrong question for a narrative-economics purpose. The tractable question is which slogan is currently spreading faster, because that is the variable actually moving retail flows, media coverage, and regulatory posture in the near term — independent of which side eventually turns out to be right.

fig.cap: Illustrative framework diagram, not observed data — a schematic of how a primary narrative and a counter-narrative can rise and mutate on staggered timelines.

sections.h: Pandemic-Era Narratives Ran as Three Competing Epidemics
ps: The COVID era produced at least three narratives running in parallel rather than in sequence: "reopen now," "this will last forever," and a set of origin-story debates about where the outbreak began. Each had its own emergence point, its own peak, and — crucially for Shiller's framework — its own mutation path once the simplest version of the slogan stopped holding attention. "Reopen" mutated into arguments about specific sectors and age groups; "this will last forever" mutated into permanent-remote-work and permanent-behavior-change variants that outlived the acute phase of the crisis itself. What makes this case instructive for operators is that the three narratives were not simply competing for accuracy — they were competing for which one got to define the decision frame for employers, venues, and policymakers at a given moment. A business that briefed only on case counts and ignored which narrative currently held the floor was, in Shiller's terms, missing half the variable that was actually moving foot traffic, staffing decisions, and event cancellations.

fig.cap: Illustrative framework diagram, not observed data — three narratives on staggered curves, illustrating how competing stories can occupy the same news cycle without converging.

sections.h: Meme-Stock Trading Turned a Story Into a Coordination Device
ps: The retail-trading surge in stocks like GameStop in January 2021 is a widely reported, real event, and it is a clean illustration of a narrative functioning as a coordination device rather than an information signal. The story — that a dispersed group of retail traders could act together against concentrated institutional short positions — did not need to be a complete or even fair account of market structure to work. It needed to be simple enough, and morally legible enough, that a large number of people could act on it at close to the same time without a central organizer. This is Shiller's "common knowledge" mechanism in its purest form: what moved the trade was not private conviction about fundamentals, but public confidence that enough other people believed the same story and were acting on it simultaneously. The narrative's economic function was coordination, not forecasting — and it is exactly the kind of case where asking "was the story true?" is less useful than asking "was the story contagious enough to synchronize behavior?"

fig.cap: Illustrative framework diagram, not observed data — a single sharp-peaked curve, the shape narrative economics predicts for a story whose primary function is coordinating simultaneous action.

title: When the Brand Outlives the House
dek: Hefner died in 2017. In 2024 his son's $100M+ bid to buy back Playboy's legacy was rejected. What survives a founder who was the product?
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: the year Hugh Hefner founded Playboy magazine
the year Hugh Hefner died
the year PLBY Group went public via SPAC merger

ps: Playboy sold a magazine, then a mansion, then a feeling of access. In 2024, seven years after Hugh Hefner's death, his son offered more than $100 million to buy the family's legacy back — and the company said no.

Hugh Hefner founded Playboy in 1953 and spent the next six decades turning it into three overlapping products: a magazine, a nightlife brand, and, by the end, a mansion that functioned as the physical showroom for all of it. Hefner died in 2017. PLBY Group, the public company that now owns the Playboy name, went public via SPAC merger in February 2021 and has run the brand since as a licensing operation — a name and a rabbit-head mark rented out across merchandise, experiences, and a relaunched magazine in what investor materials describe as roughly 180 countries. Read against each other, the four dates on this timeline compress seventy-one years into three transitions: six decades building a founder-fused hospitality brand, then a four-year gap between Hefner's death and the company's SPAC listing, then three more years before the board had to decide, in public, what kind of company it actually was.

fig.cap: Sixty-four years of founder-fused brand-building preceded a decision made in three years of public-company math — the board's answer favored the licensing shell over the family buyback.

sections.h: The Founder Problem: When the CEO Was the Catalog
ps: Brands that fuse founder and product face a specific kind of balance-sheet exposure that ordinary consumer brands do not: the company cannot simply "rebrand the CEO" when the CEO was, for decades, the catalog itself. Hugh Hefner's late-life reputation has become part of the mark's baggage rather than an asset the company can still activate — he is not available to appear, endorse, or update the brand's meaning. PLBY Group's licensing thesis is, in effect, an attempt to keep the commercial value of the mark — the name, the bunny, the built-up recognition in roughly 180 countries — while distancing the operating business from the household that originally generated it.

In 2024, Cooper Hefner made a cash-plus-equity offer reported at more than $100 million, framed publicly as an attempt to reacquire the family's legacy assets. The PLBY board rejected the offer, stating it undervalued the company's assets under the continuing licensing model — Variety's reporting on the bid is the primary account of both the offer and the board's stated reasoning. The conflict at the center of that rejection is the chapter hinge of this report: heritage nostalgia, the framing behind Cooper Hefner's bid, against an asset-light profit-and-loss model built on licensing a mark whose living, personal referent is no longer available to the business. The board's decision did not resolve that tension philosophically. It resolved it commercially, in a single dated boardroom vote, in the company's favor as a licensing operation rather than as a returned family heirloom.

sections.h: A Gag That Outlived the Product
ps: One small, dated fact shows how long the mansion myth kept circulating in mainstream culture after the hospitality product itself had peaked. In Illumination's animated film Hop, released in 2011, Russell Brand voiced the lead rabbit character E.B., in a plot that includes a stylized Playboy Mansion-style setting; Hugh Hefner voiced a cameo role in the same film. This is a children's-film voice-cast credit, not a claim about anyone's conduct, and it is cited here strictly as cultural sediment — evidence that the Playboy Mansion, as an idea, had enough mainstream recognition in 2011 to work as a family-movie reference point, years before the founder's death and a decade before the company became a public licensing shell.

Playboy's founder built a brand where the product and the person were, for most of its history, difficult to separate. The 2024 rejection of Cooper Hefner's $100 million-plus bid is a modest but legible answer to what survives a founder like that: not the household, and not a family-run return to the mansion era, but a licensed mark the current business believes is worth more running as a licensing operation than handed back as legacy. Whether that mark keeps clearing in roughly 180 countries without a living founder attached to it is a question this single decision does not settle — it only shows what the board decided it was worth betting on in 2024.

title: What Star Risk Costs an IP
dek: Merch built Pokémon's $91B; one actor's six films show the bill.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: Pokémon lifetime revenue (largest single property row in the franchise file)
Share of row-sum revenue from merchandise, licensing & retail (recomputed from franchise.csv)
Median domestic gross across 3,401 films in the horror-tagged dataset

ps: Merchandise-driven IP and star-fronted vehicles do not carry the same economic risk. The TidyTuesday 2019-07-02 media-franchise file lists 103 properties with Wikipedia lifetime revenue estimates (mid-2019); Pokémon leads at $91B, and merchandise, licensing, and retail account for 56% of row-sum revenue in the committed CSV — the same figures published in Artometrics' franchise report. When most of the money attaches to characters and products, a weak theatrical run is a line item, not an existential bet.

sections.h: Merchandise Is the Insulation IP Franchises Have and Star Vehicles Don't
ps: Artometrics' franchise-revenue report established that merchandise is not one revenue stream among several — it is the dominant one, at 56% of row-sum revenue across 103 franchise rows in the TidyTuesday extract (61% and a count of 107 appeared in earlier published copy). Pokémon's $91B total, the highest of any tracked property, was built almost entirely on cards, games, and retail rather than any theatrical run. Henry Jenkins's transmedia framework (Convergence Culture, NYU Press, 2006) helps explain why: revenue attached to a character or mascot can move across games, apparel, and film without routing through a single performer's weekend gross. Contrast that with a franchise or vehicle built around one performer's draw. When merchandise, licensing, and games are absent or minor, the entire revenue case rests on box office and, downstream, on home video and streaming licensing tied to that same theatrical result. There is no secondary economy running in parallel the way there is for Pokémon or, per the same report, for Star Wars — the one franchise in that dataset the report specifically flagged as fully diversified across box office, merchandise, home video, and games. A star-fronted film without that diversification is, in revenue-structure terms, closer to a single bet than to a franchise.

fig.cap: Merchandise, licensing, and retail account for 56% of row-sum revenue across 103 franchise rows — a stream that does not depend on any one actor's box office weekend.

sections.h: What Concentrated Star Risk Looks Like: A Six-Film Case Study
ps: The case-study dataset is small and deliberately narrow: six of actor Jared Leto's 2020s film credits, each expressed as worldwide gross divided by reported production budget, using trade-reported budget bands from Box Office Mojo. House of Gucci (2021, ensemble) returned 2.04x on a $75M budget. Morbius (2022, lead) returned 2.02x on $83M. Those two clear breakeven with room. The other four sit closer to the line or under it: The Little Things (2021, lead, released into a pandemic-narrowed theatrical window) landed at 1.03x; Haunted Mansion (2023, ensemble) at 0.79x; Masters of the Universe (2026, supporting) at 0.66x; and Tron: Ares (2025, lead) at 0.65x, on the largest reported budget in the slate at $220M. Read individually, each figure is a data point about one film. Read as a slate, the pattern is a distribution centered near or below 1.0x rather than comfortably above it — half the titles below breakeven, and only two of six clearing 2.0x. That is the shape of concentrated star risk: revenue tied tightly to one theatrical outcome per title, with no licensing or merchandise base underneath it the way Pokémon's $91B or Star Wars' diversified mix has. When a title in this kind of slate underperforms, the studio absorbs the loss directly — there is no secondary revenue stream to blunt it. This is a small, non-random sample, and the report treats it as illustration, not proof; see Limitations below.

fig.cap: Three of six titles in the case-study slate clear breakeven comfortably; three land at or below 1.0x — a spread with no merchandise layer to soften it.

ps: Editorial framework, not measured finding: the evidence assembled here is consistent with the idea that merchandise-driven IP carries structurally less exposure to any one person's performance than a star-fronted vehicle does. The six-film case study illustrates concentrated theatrical exposure when that cushion is absent — not proof about any particular result. De Vany and Walls (2004) show why theatrical outcomes alone behave like lottery tickets; this report asks whether merchandise share is the hedge studios buy when they want something sturdier than a lottery ticket. A future report with a larger sample could test whether merchandise share predicts how much a single underperforming title costs the studio that owns it.

title: When Flops End Hollywood's Silence
dek: BBC's Leto exposé asks why not sooner. Six film ROIs and four institutional cases test what forward value has to do with it.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: Tron: Ares (2025) worldwide gross ÷ reported budget, Leto's most recent lead role
Masters of the Universe (2026) gross ÷ budget in a supporting role
Morbius (2022) and House of Gucci (2021), the two 2020s titles that cleared their budgets twice over

ps: BBC News and the July 2026 documentary Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret reported criminal sexual conduct allegations from multiple women against the actor; Leto denies the allegations. The public question that follows a belated exposé is almost always the same one: why not sooner? Artometrics asks a colder, answerable version of it instead: what was he still worth?

This report does not adjudicate the allegations, and it draws no conclusion about their truth. It tests a narrower, economic hypothesis against public box-office data and the record of four earlier cases in which an institution eventually stopped protecting a person it had shielded: Harvey Weinstein, Bryan Singer, Jimmy Savile, and Russell Brand. In each case, allegations against a living or deceased public figure are described using allegation-and-denial language, except where a criminal conviction or an official public inquiry has already settled the record. Both cases sit outside the "declining studio asset" logic that fits Weinstein reasonably well. Savile was never dropped at all — the institution's failure was total and only corrected after death and an official inquiry. Brand's case shows how the model breaks down further once the "institution" is no longer a single employer with a P&L to protect.

fig.cap: A proposed framework, not a proven index: where each case sits on institution type and prior commercial decline.

ps: This section is an editorial framework, not a statistically tested finding. The chart below places four cases on two proposed axes: whether the person's forward commercial value had already declined before public exposure, and whether the protecting institution is a commercial studio pricing a bankable asset or a broadcaster selling institutional trust. Weinstein sits at "studio, already declining" — the cleanest fit for a threshold story. Savile sits at "broadcaster, not declining" — protection that never broke on its own. Singer sits in between: a studio-adjacent case where a hit film complicated, but ultimately did not reverse, the collapse that followed a second exposé. Leto is plotted as an open question: a 2020s slate that is softening but mixed, inside a studio system, at the moment the BBC's reporting arrived. Reading this map honestly requires holding two things at once. The pattern it shows — protection breaking earlier when there is less left to lose, and holding longer when the product is trust rather than a slate — fits the two cleanest cases well. It fits Singer only partly, and it says nothing yet about Leto beyond describing where his commercial position stood at the moment reporting on the allegations against him arrived.

The honest version of this report's finding is modest. Jared Leto's 2020s film slate had already softened — three straight titles below break-even on trade-reported figures — by the time the BBC's July 2026 documentary reported allegations against him. That fact alone proves nothing about timing or motive. What the four comparison cases add is a sharper question rather than an answer: institutional protection appears to track forward commercial value more legibly when the institution is a studio pricing a bankable asset (Weinstein) than when it is a broadcaster selling trust (Savile), and a single hit film is not proof that protection has resumed (Singer). Where Leto's case falls on that map is, for now, an open question this report is built to keep asking rather than to close.

title: Record Sale, No Championship Formula
dek: José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones paid a record $3.9bn for a club drawing 42,000 a game, ranked last in farm talent, and carrying $858m owed to five underperforming stars.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: Record baseball sale price — 26% premium to Forbes' $3.1bn March valuation on $484m revenue
Michael King and Mason Miller combined — cost $21m while five stars owed $858m produced 4.5
Farm system rank of 30 clubs — emptied by trading Leo De Vries for Mason Miller in July 2025

ps: The most expensive baseball team ever sold has the emptiest farm system in the sport, $858m owed to five players, and no regional television network.

José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones agreed in May 2026 to pay $3.9bn for the San Diego Padres—a 26% premium to Forbes' $3.1bn March valuation, which was based on estimated revenue of $484m and operating income of roughly $20m. The arithmetic is eight times revenue for a club in the 30th-largest media market in the United States. The Dodgers are the immediate obstacle and cannot be outspent: back-to-back champions, roughly twice San Diego's revenue, thirteen games clear in the division. Milwaukee is the more instructive comparison—67-40 this season on a $124m Opening Day payroll, built almost entirely through internal development. San Diego has spent five years trying to beat Los Angeles at its own game on a fifth of its local media revenue, while running Milwaukee's problem in reverse. The championship-asset index is editorial, not a model. It scores five dimensions on a 0-100 scale to make the shape of the gap legible; the inputs are valuation, tax payroll, share of value from controlled players, published farm rankings, and postseason results since 2020.

fig.cap: Where new ownership should spend its first year

sections.h: The memo: six moves, in order
ps: The instinct at this price will be a statement signing. It is the wrong first move: the roster's marginal need is not another $300m bat. In rough order of urgency: 1. Refund the pipeline as a capital project, not a scouting line. Spend the full draft and international bonus pools, buy development infrastructure, and hire away the staff that rival clubs use to turn marginal prospects into major leaguers. It is the cheapest source of wins in the sport and the only one that compounds. It is also the item the outgoing regime spent. 2. Buy innings, not headliners. The rotation has been carried by King through a summer in which the salary sitting on the injured list has been the ninth-largest in baseball. October is decided by a club's fourth and fifth-best pitchers, which is the category San Diego has never bought and the one available cheaply every winter. 3. Fix the October offense deliberately. The last two eliminations were failures to score: shut out over the final two games of the 2024 division series, five runs across three games in 2025. This lineup is built on power and aggression, a profile that fails against elite pitching in short series. On-base skill and contact are the missing inputs, and they cost less than power does. 4. Treat local media as a business you own. Seventy thousand direct subscribers is the biggest such base in baseball and it was assembled in three seasons out of a bankruptcy. Own the funnel, price it properly, and extend it across the border rather than waiting for a regional network that is not coming back. 5. Extend Miller; treat Merrill as untouchable. Both are cheap, both are in their twenties, and neither can be replaced from within this system. Buying out Miller's arbitration years fixes a cost curve for four seasons; trading him fixes a quarter. 6. Settle governance before the winter. Feliciano will be the control person and intends to run the club in partnership with Jones. The most valuable document they can produce internally is the mandate: one decision-maker for baseball, one time horizon, one definition of success. The Seidler era's strength was clarity of purpose; its weakness was that the purpose outlived the plan for achieving it.

sections.h: The arithmetic of a first title
ps: San Diego does not have a 90-win problem. It reached the postseason five times from 2020 through 2026, including a wild-card sweep of the Cubs, and left without a pennant every time. The 2026 exit was a division-series loss to the Brewers.

Closing that gap is not a payroll exercise, which is fortunate, because payroll is the one lever this club has already pulled to its limit. It is a depth-and-pipeline exercise, and those are the two things a recapitalized franchise can buy quickly—if the owners spend on infrastructure rather than announcements.

title: The Cost of Controlling the House
dek: A Psychonomics profile of Beyoncé — Hermann Leadership Trait Analysis, Parkwood as institutionalized self, Lemonade’s canon economics, and an 8,000-line lyric machine.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: Expert-coded Task Orientation (T) under Hermann (1999) LTA — the highest spike in this profile
Belief in Ability to Control Events (B) — surprise-album and Parkwood ownership signature
Lemonade’s rank on the Rolling Stone 500 (2020 list) in the Artometrics album file

ps: Economics comes from the Greek oikonomia — the management of the house. Psychonomics asks the prior question: who is managing the soul of the house, and what does their inner architecture cost everyone living inside it? The founding Artometrics case was Julius Caesar: a leader who treated the self as the institution, extended trust freely, and was removed by the highest-centrality nodes in his own patronage graph.

Beyoncé Knowles-Carter is the entertainment-industry case for the same method. Born in 1981, solo debut album year 2003 in the Artometrics Rolling Stone file, she is not a head of state. She is a head of catalog — and of Parkwood Entertainment, the firm she founded in 2010 to keep authorship, touring, and filmed spectacle under one roof (Parkwood Entertainment). The psychonomic claim of this report is specific: where Caesar’s theory was magnanimous personal power without redundancy, Beyoncé’s theory is owned control of the creative house, paired with an affiliation-dense public voice and a spectacle-heavy measurable catalog.

Beyoncé’s coded profile spikes on Task Orientation (T = 0.91) and Belief in Ability to Control Events (B = 0.88), with Need for Power (P = 0.86) and Conceptual Complexity (CC = 0.82) also well above the world-leader baseline. In-group bias (IB = 0.78) and Need for Affiliation (A = 0.74) sit high. Distrust of others (D = 0.62) is above baseline (0.48) — the opposite direction from Caesar’s D = 0.31.

That asymmetry is the psychonomic argument. Caesar’s dangerous triangle was ceiling power + floor distrust: convert everyone, absorb the Republic into the self, die by the inner ring. Beyoncé’s triangle is ceiling task/control + mid-high distrust + high affiliation: speak in “we,” build a fandom institution, but do not outsource authorship governance to rivals you have pardoned into the center. The public voice is warm; the firm boundary is cold.

The Artometrics Rolling Stone albums file carries two Beyoncé studio albums on the 2020 RS500 list. The 2013 self-titled album: Billboard peak #1, 186 weeks on chart, Spotify popularity 75, RS rank #81, artist age-at-list ~32. Lemonade (2016): peak #1, 87 weeks, Spotify popularity 73, RS rank #32, age-at-list ~35. Debut album year in that file: 2003.

Caesar’s patronage chart had every edge terminating on a person. Beyoncé’s chart has a second center of gravity: Parkwood Entertainment — the firm that converts personal authorship into an institution that can sign, stage, and film without surrendering the name. Family (JAY-Z, Blue Ivy), formative group (Destiny’s Child circle), major-label distribution, live spectacle (Coachella → Homecoming), feature peers, and the Beyhive all connect — but governance weight sits on the Parkwood edge.

The packaged Artometrics extract holds 8,000 lyric lines across 139 song entities (~61.8k tokens, ~3,150 types). Top content signals are relational and imperative: love 543, baby 457, boy 283, girl 239, night 104. Identity/place markers appear at lower but non-trivial rates (black 59, texas 18). Abstract power language is scarce (power 5, queen 9).

Among 139 song entities in the extract: 35 carry Ft. credits, 35 are live/awards/“Experience”-type performance documents, 19 are remixes, and 64 fall outside those flags. Top line-count entities include VMA performance text and a Destiny’s Child medley — long spectacle documents, not three-minute singles. Collaboration titles skew toward JAY-Z, with additional peers (Kanye West, Pharrell Williams, Nicki Minaj, and others) as catalog edges rather than co-governors.

Beyoncé’s Psychonomics profile is a high-control, high-task, affiliation-forward leadership shape with Parkwood as the institutionalized self. The economic fingerprint splits commercial longevity (self-titled’s 186 Billboard weeks) from canon elevation (Lemonade at RS #32). The lyric machine sells belonging; the firm keeps the keys. Compared with Caesar, the innovation is structural: distrust is high enough to keep knives out of the inner ring, and the house is built to be owned, not merely personally held.

title: A ¥10.3 Million Win Becomes Cultural Reckoning
dek: Louis Vuitton won ¥10.3 million against Molly Tea in Suzhou court on 29 June 2026 for four-petal logo infringement. Chinese social media reframed the first-to-file trademark case as foreign enclosure of Tang-era motifs.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: First-instance damages and costs awarded to Louis Vuitton; judgment is not final
LV trademark-infringement records in China over five years (media-cited Qichacha tally)
Four-petal flower trademarks held infringed by the Suzhou court

ps: A Suzhou trademark judgment awarded Louis Vuitton ¥10.3 million against a domestic tea chain. Chinese social media turned the ruling into a morality play about cultural theft. The court record is narrower: Louis Vuitton Malletier sued Shenzhen Molly Tea over a four-petal floral device used in brand identity, the first-instance court found infringement of seven registered marks, and Molly Tea announced an appeal.
This report separates what the judgment and CNIPA history show, how the case fits Louis Vuitton's broader China enforcement pattern, and why a legally ordinary win became a cultural-economy event.

The first-instance order requires Shenzhen Molly Tea to cease infringing use of the disputed four-petal device, pay ¥10 million in economic damages and ¥300,000 in reasonable enforcement costs, and publish corrective statements on six surfaces: official website, Weibo, WeChat Official Account, WeChat Mini Program, Xiaohongshu, and Douyin. A franchise defendant was described as jointly liable up to ¥100,000. Molly Tea publicly announced an appeal.

Two procedural facts matter. First, Molly Tea had tried to register a four-petal logo; CNIPA refused application no. 81049590 (Class 43), citing prior LV flower marks, and the refusal review became final. Second, the court's association logic sits in a market where luxury–FMCG collaborations are common — so "nobody confuses a handbag with milk tea" misses the legal question, which was whether the logo could suggest sponsorship or commercial linkage.

Chinese coverage places Molly Tea inside a multi-year Louis Vuitton enforcement campaign: approximately 1,691 trademark-infringement records over five years, with 56 new filings reported in the first half of 2026. Recoveries across many matters are described as modest relative to global luxury revenue — deterrence and anti-dilution, not a profit center.

That context cuts both ways. It undercuts the idea that Molly Tea was a one-off bullying novelty: LV litigates flower-device conflicts as portfolio practice. It also explains why the public read this case as the tip of a pattern — especially when parallel administrative fights with CNIPA and other small defendants entered the same news cycle. Comparative China brand fights (for example, long-running New Balance mark disputes or the Dior / mamianqun controversy) show the same structural tension: first-to-file commercial exclusivity versus popular claims about shared cultural forms.

Xiaohongshu and state-media posts placed LV's four-petal monogram flower beside Tang-dynasty decoration — rosewood pipa inlay and quatrefoil window lattice in classical gardens such as Suzhou's Humble Administrator's Garden. Historians describe baoxiang motifs as composite ornamental vocabularies drawn from lotus, peony, and related flora. Persimmon-calyx geometry is another folk visual rhyme circulating in the same threads.

Those comparisons establish visual kinship in a shared decorative commons. They do not cancel a registered commercial graphic under China's Trademark Law. LV's own origin story for the 1896 Monogram, as relayed in LVMH materials and wire reporting, cites neo-gothic ornament and Japonism — not a court finding that the mark is a Tang-era replica.

sections.h: Secondary-market signal, not a balance sheet
ps: Chinese secondary-market coverage after the judgment described quieter boutiques and softer ask prices — for example, a Carryall small near ¥19,000 new on Dewu against ~¥23,000 retail, and deeper discounts on used Neverfull and Onthego units. Dealers also described a surge of sellers. That is a real market mood.

In the court frame, registered rights, CNIPA prior refusal, and association risk dominate. In the public frame, Tang resemblance, nationalist brand optics, and "foreign giant vs domestic chain" narrative dominate. East Is Read's media monitoring put related posts in the hundreds of thousands with Weibo topic pages in the hundreds of millions of views — order-of-magnitude attention, not legal error.

Molly Tea is a first-instance trademark defendant ordered to pay ¥10.3 million and apologize on six platforms; the case is on appeal. Louis Vuitton's legal theory sits inside a large China enforcement machine. The internet's theory sits inside a longer argument about who may exclusively commercialize motifs that also live in Chinese decorative history. The viral Shorts are a map of popular feeling, not a substitute for the docket.

title: Netflix's Top 10% of Titles Drew 68% of Viewing
dek: Netflix's January–June 2026 engagement report lists 17,370 titles with at least 50,000 views worldwide (8,193 shows and 9,177 movies). The top 10% drew 67.9% of named hours; the top 20% drew 82.6%.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: titles with at least 50,000 views worldwide in Jan–Jun 2026 (8,193 shows, 9,177 movies)
of named hours from the top 10% of titles; the top 20% drew 82.6%
No public dataset measures homepage promotion or how many properties are marketed in a quarter

ps: Netflix's What We Watched report for January–June 2026 lists 17,370 titles with at least 50,000 views worldwide — 8,193 shows and 9,177 movies — and 96.80 billion named hours. The top 10% of those titles drew 67.9% of named hours, and the top 20% drew 82.6%. No public dataset measures homepage promotion or how many properties a platform markets in a quarter.

This report measures how viewing concentrated across that disclosed list, and how many of those titles also appeared on Netflix's weekly global Top 10. Target readers: analysts tracking platform strategy, researchers studying attention economics, and editors covering media consolidation.

How to read this report: Each chart caption states the finding first, then the measurement method. Numbers marked "observed" come directly from source data; "derived" metrics are calculated aggregates. Check the limitations section before citing any figure.

sections.h: HOW BIG IS THE LIBRARY — AND HOW TOP-HEAVY?
ps: Of the 17,370 named titles, the top 10% drew 67.9% of named hours and the top 20% drew 82.6%. The bottom half of titles drew 3.2% of named hours. The curves separate shows from movies, counting each title's share within its own kind.

Named titles exclude the Other Shows and Other Movies rows. Those rows cover viewing of titles under 50,000 views, and video podcasts are included under Other Shows, so the named hours are not 100% of viewing on Netflix in the half.

fig.cap: The top 10% of named titles drew 67.9% of hours in January–June 2026, and the top 20% drew 82.6%. Cumulative share of titles, largest first, against share of hours, with Shows and Movies as separate lines. 17,370 titles (8,193 shows and 9,177 movies).

sections.h: CONCENTRATION: WHO OWNS THE MIDDLE OF THE SHELF?
ps: Neither Netflix file names a studio or a rights holder. The engagement report does mark whether a title was Available Globally. Titles marked yes were 30.4% of named titles and 47.0% of named hours.
That column is Netflix's availability flag, not a measure of ownership. No public dataset measures homepage placement.

fig.cap: Titles Netflix marked Available Globally were 30.4% of named titles and 47.0% of named hours. This is Netflix's availability flag, not ownership.

sections.h: THE AVAILABILITY GAP: HYPE VS WHAT STAYS UP
ps: Titles that appeared on a weekly global Top 10 in the weeks ending January 4 through June 28, 2026 were 2.8% of named titles and drew 26.6% of named hours. Of the 100 most-watched named titles, 29 never appeared on those lists.

Only global lists were checked, and titles were matched by name. One charted name did not match: the Top 10 file lists "Furies: Season 2: : Resistance" (a double colon), while the engagement report lists "Furies: Season 2: Furies: Resistance." 488 of 489 charted names matched. No public dataset measures which titles a recommendation system repeats.

fig.cap: Hours viewed against weeks on the global Top 10, weeks ending January 4 through June 28, 2026. Only global lists were checked, and titles were matched by name. 29 of the 100 most-watched titles never charted.

ps: On this list, a small share of titles carries most of the viewing: the top 10% drew 67.9% of named hours, and the top 20% drew 82.6%. Titles that reached the global Top 10 were 2.8% of the list and 26.6% of named hours.

The best use of these charts is to sharpen questions about platform strategy and attention economics, not to make claims about homepage promotion, marketing spend, or content quality. Those are not in this file. Check the source notes before citing any figure.

title: What Does Your Country Sell?
dek: Export ledgers reveal national identity under market constraint—200+ countries, 5,000+ products, six diagnostic questions.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: Countries and zones covered in UN Comtrade systems, revealing what the world buys from each
Products classified under OEC Harmonized System codes, separating complexity from commodity
Diagnostic questions that turn export data into identity analysis, from substitutability to prestige

ps: What a nation sells abroad is one of the few identity claims that must clear a market test. Tourism slogans can invent a self-image; export ledgers record what other countries will actually pay for.

UN Comtrade and OEC systems track 200+ countries and zones and 5,000+ products under Harmonized System codes. The atlas below uses 6 diagnostic questions to make identity readable without pretending the indices are final official rankings.

Scale and complexity are different virtues. A country can be large because it sells one thing in volume, or complex because it sells many hard-to-make things. Those identities behave differently under shock.

Exports reveal what a country can reliably make and sell into the world. Scale and complexity are different axes: volume without sophistication is one identity; sophistication without volume is another; both together is rarer. Countries plotted high on both dimensions occupy a different strategic neighborhood from resource giants that score high on scale alone. The chart stops those neighborhoods from being collapsed into a single big-exporter label.

fig.cap: Countries differ by export scale and product complexity

ps: Cars, electronics, oil, pharmaceuticals, aircraft, software, agriculture, and textiles are not just commodities. They become reputational shorthand—Germany and machines, Saudi Arabia and energy, the United States and software services. Exports become part of national mythology when they are repeated long enough to feel like character. The data still matter because mythology that loses market share eventually becomes nostalgia.

fig.cap: Some export categories become national symbols

ps: The last generation of globalization did not erase goods. It added services, software, intellectual property, finance, and standards to the frontier. Manufacturing indices that peak and then soften while services and IP climb are the signature of that shift. A modern country atlas must therefore track both containers and code. An economy that only reports tonnage will misread its own power—and its own vulnerability.

fig.cap: The frontier moved from resources to factories to systems and IP

ps: Germany and Japan can look similar through machines and vehicles, while Brazil and Saudi Arabia show very different resource and food signatures. The fingerprint is the mix across machines, vehicles, chemicals, resources, food, and services—not a single headline product. The question is not only what a place sells. It is what would break if the world stopped buying it, and what prestige categories would remain even if volume fell.

The atlas ends with vulnerability questions: what does the country sell, who buys it, what inputs does it need, what could replace it, what carries prestige, and what is vulnerable? Those six prompts turn trade tables into identity analysis. Countries that cannot answer them with data are flying blind about their own external face. Countries that answer only with slogans are doing public relations, not strategy.
Exports are identity under constraint. They show what a country can do at scale, what the world believes it is good for, and where substitution would hurt.
Later comparison work can rank places by complexity, concentration, cultural export power, and substitutability—but only after the fingerprint and the six diagnostic questions are in view.

title: A Data Framework for Economic Identity
dek: 1,667 subnational regions and 1,100+ datasets define the economic signature of cities — exports, housing, transit, culture, and historical infrastructure.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: Subnational regions in DOSE v2.14 provide global coverage for cross-city economic comparison
Cities in World Cities Culture Forum 5th edition enable cultural infrastructure benchmarking
Datasets in DataSF public portal supply granular local system data

ps: 1,667 subnational regions in DOSE v2.14 and 1,100+ datasets in DataSF establish a system map for cities—what they export, import, price out, and preserve through infrastructure. This framework separates economic identity from promotional narrative with six diagnostic questions and eight system layers drawn from BEA regional GDP, DOSE global subnational output, World Cities Culture Forum, Census ACS, and local Socrata portals. The approach treats cities as layered machines—firms, ports, universities, housing, cultural venues, finance, infrastructure, rules, and stories—before any city-to-city comparison.

A city is not one industry. It is a layered machine: firms, ports, universities, housing, cultural venues, finance, infrastructure, rules, and stories. The first question is not whether a city is good. It is what kind of system the city is trying to be.

fig.cap: A city identity is a stack of economic and cultural systems

ps: Houston and Los Angeles still have obvious goods and logistics signatures. New York and San Francisco sell more invisible products: finance, software, expertise, media, and market access. Invisible exports are harder to observe but often define the city's price structure.

fig.cap: Some cities export goods while others export coordination, code, finance, or attention

ps: History is infrastructure that keeps generating data: street grids, warehouses, universities, firm clusters, zoning, and migration patterns. A city report should identify which older layer is still driving current performance.

fig.cap: Ports, factories, corporate headquarters, and software leave measurable shadows

ps: One variable lies. A fingerprint requires a pattern. The same GDP level can mean very different things under different housing, transit, culture, and export structures. A city profile should read like a data portrait, not a fact sheet.

Before building comparisons, the local report needs its diagnostic questions. What does the place make? What does it import? What is scarce? Which cities are its real competitors? Those questions turn open data into an identity argument.
Cities generate data signatures. The challenge is separating slogan from system: what is produced, what is scarce, who competes, and what historical layer still controls the present.
This framework gives future city reports a repeatable structure before deeper city-to-city comparisons.

title: How Movies Become IMDb Famous
dek: Title fields, ratings, and box-office references explain how films accumulate attention.
author: Kyle McAuliffe

kp.l: Core IMDb non-commercial TSV files publicly documented
IMDb dataset refresh cadence
Genres can be listed per IMDb title basics row

ps: Movies are perfect Artometrics objects because they are art, market, memory, and industrial strategy at the same time. A title page on IMDb is where those forces leave public footprints: genres, runtimes, ratings, and vote counts.

The question is what a blockbuster is mathematically — attention, rating, runtime, franchise memory, platform behavior, and studio grammar stacked into one cultural event. The pieces below treat IMDb’s non-commercial dataset architecture as a scoreboard for that grammar, with box-office and platform references for context.

Seven core TSV files are publicly documented; the refresh cadence is daily. Up to three genres can appear per title-basics row. Avatar’s runtime sits at 162 minutes. An illustrative 69% sequel/franchise share among top hits in the 2020s frames the sequelization chart; five charts carry the argument.

IMDb-style datasets are useful because ratings and vote counts separate two behaviors: how many people cared enough to rate, and how positively they scored the title. The blockbuster problem starts there. Popularity is not quality, but quality without attention rarely becomes culture. Genre charts that pair those axes make the split legible.

fig.cap: Genre attention and audience rating tell different stories

ps: The blockbuster increasingly behaves like a portfolio asset. Studios learned that recognition lowers marketing risk, so the cultural market tilts toward sequels, universes, and repeatable IP — the illustrative 69% franchise share among recent top hits is a directional marker of that tilt. This is not just nostalgia. It is risk management drawn as culture.

fig.cap: The hit movie became a serial product

ps: A common hypothesis says shorter attention spans should punish long films. The evidence is messier: the event movie can still stretch past two or three hours if the social reward is high enough — Avatar’s 162 minutes is a familiar case of time granted as prestige. The runtime question is really a trust question. Audiences give time when they believe the movie is an event.

fig.cap: Event movies can ask audiences for more time

ps: A theater ticket once created a clean cultural signal: you went somewhere, paid, and joined an audience. Streaming makes discovery easier but ownership fuzzier. That is why the modern hit can feel huge and disposable at the same time — visible everywhere, belonging nowhere in particular.

Disney’s modern advantage is not simply scale. It is the ability to convert characters, brands, parks, merchandise, and streaming into one IP flywheel. A24 represents the opposite grammar: smaller, identity-heavy, taste-based cultural capital. Studios differ in how much they depend on franchise logic — and those differences show up as different scoreboard shapes.
The blockbuster is not one variable. It is the agreement between attention, trust, platform, and industrial repetition.
The most useful next step is a true title-level pipeline: join title basics, ratings, box office, awards, and streaming availability, then let each movie explain its own path to fame.
